corpus_observations: The pack is dominated by three recurring genres: cold intros anchored on peer customers ("Working with Onfido, Veriff & others"), invitations to exec dinners/mixers ("[Invite] Encord AI Leaders Dinner @ Kokkari 02/27"), and conference meetup asks ("Attending CVPR | quick coffee?"). Template reuse is heavy and visible: several bodies appear verbatim to different recipients with only the name/company swapped (emails 9/79/89/98, 10/93, 33/70, 48/51/63, 82/86, 23/49, 32/38), and reusable blocks like "Bit of context on Encord...we're a computer vision scale-up (recently raised a $30M Series B)" recur across senders. Mail-merge residue and typos are common enough to be a real axis of variation ("Hi ,", "Assuming you and the Christian team will be in Nashville", "Email: charlotte@encord.com: mailto:youremail@encord.com", "if you're be open", "private dinning room", "Muck like them"). At the same time, a meaningful minority show genuine per-recipient research ("I recently read that Outrider has addressed over 200,000 safety scenarios", "I just listened to your interview w/ Bulk Exchanges") and warm hooks via colleagues or prior contact. A handful of items are not true first-touch outbound at all (mid-thread replies, rescheduling, onboarding kick-off, an internal security-questionnaire forward: emails 6, 8, 26, 36, 57, 78, 80, 92), which any judging pipeline should expect and possibly filter.

dimensions.name: Recipient-specific research signal
dimensions.definition: How much the email demonstrates concrete, checkable knowledge of this recipient or their company (products, news, talks, hires, filings) versus knowledge that could apply to anyone in the vertical. Judged only from what is asserted in the text, not its truth.
dimensions.variation_seen: Wide variation. High: "I recently read that Outrider has addressed over 200,000 safety scenarios — an impressive stat that speaks to the scale and complexity of your ML systems" (email 62) or "I just listened to your interview w/ Bulk Exchanges - v inspired by your vision to automate heavy machinery" (41). Low: the blank-merge "Hi ," opener with only "I browsed your website" (5), and the broken merge "Assuming you and the Christian team will be in Nashville for CVPR" (63) — the recipient's first name pasted where the company should be.

dimensions.name: Trigger / 'why now' rationale
dimensions.definition: Whether the email states an explicit, dated reason this outreach is happening now — funding round, product launch, hiring post, conference attendance, a referral conversation — versus no stated occasion.
dimensions.variation_seen: High: "Congrats on your Series A announcement! I saw you're hiring an engineer to scale your annotation infrastructure" (74), "I noticed you're attending NeurIPS this year" (46), "Flexiv's came up during a chat with 1X at our Physical AI event in SF last week" (60). Low: "Great to see that you were exploring Encord - wanted to reach out to see if I could help with anything?" (47) and the generic "1-1 meeting with Encord?" website-visitor chaser (0), which cite no occasion beyond a page visit.

dimensions.name: Specificity of the value claim
dimensions.definition: Whether the benefit Encord promises is quantified and mechanism-specific versus abstract platform language. Concrete numbers, named capabilities, and named failure modes score high; slogans score low.
dimensions.variation_seen: High: "How StandardAI increased annotation throughput by 5x with Encord - saving $600k annually" and "eliminates ghost frames / sync issues vs frame-by-frame approach" (1); "typically delivering a 5-10x improvement in annotation speed" (24); "label data 2x-10x faster than in-house or first gen tools" (62). Low: "Designed to streamline data management and accelerate model development... I believe there's potential for synergy as you scale" (20) and "built to help teams bring better models to market, faster" (37, 48, and elsewhere verbatim).

dimensions.name: Relevance of social proof to the recipient
dimensions.definition: Not whether customers are name-dropped (nearly all emails do) but whether the named companies are in the recipient's own vertical and framed as 'your peers', versus a stock all-purpose list. The recipient's domain is usually inferable from the email itself.
dimensions.variation_seen: High: to a driver-monitoring company, "we're working w/ a few of your peers (SmartEye, Nauto, Netradyne, Seeing Machines, Woven by Toyota, Nexar, etc)... driver behavior analytics, in-cabin monitoring" (27); to ID-verification firms, "We've recently started working with Onfido, Veriff & iProov" (9/79/98). Low: the same stock trio "including Synthesia, Hudl, and Woven by Toyota" sent to ZEISS, EarthCam and others regardless of domain (48, 51, 63).

dimensions.name: Problem-narrative specificity
dimensions.definition: Whether the email articulates a concrete, plausible pain in the recipient's workflow (with details of how it manifests) versus asserting a generic assumed need ('as you scale...').
dimensions.variation_seen: High: "existing data curation & visualisation solutions (Voxel51 & internal tools)... lacking the speed & scalability required to efficiently search through their training datasets (capping out at ~1m images)" (56); "fine-tuning models for new stores was frustratingly slow and expensive - given bottlenecks in coordinating between CV teams and their third-party annotation partners" (69). Low: "As your AI team grows, I imagine you are handling massive volumes of data that need to flow seamlessly through your annotation workflows" (20).

dimensions.name: Clarity and concreteness of the ask
dimensions.definition: Whether the email ends with one unambiguous call to action the recipient can answer with yes/no plus a time, versus a vague or hedged close. Concrete proposed slots score highest; 'worth connecting?' and 'let me know if you have questions' score low.
dimensions.variation_seen: High: "Proposing some time for a quick platform demo on Thursday 26th at 1pm ET" (1); "Next Tuesday 12.30-2pm and Wednesday 2-3pm (Israel Time) are open right now" (52); "I'm flexible Tuesday to Thursday if you're open to a chat" (19). Low: "Would it be worth us connecting?" as the entire close (9, 79, 81, 98) and "Curious to explore how we can help the Motional team - let me know if you have any questions" (10, 93), which asks for nothing schedulable.

dimensions.name: Size of the ask
dimensions.definition: The magnitude of commitment requested, as stated in the text: quick reply or booth drop-by, 15/20-minute call, 30-minute chat, platform demo, or a multi-hour in-person dinner/event. Distinct from clarity — an ask can be clear but large.
dimensions.variation_seen: The corpus spans the full range: "if you have 15 mins to chat over the coming weeks" (33), "a 20-mins chat tomorrow or Friday" (44), "a 30-minute chat this week or the next" (3, 27, 97), a demo plus follow-up (1), up to three-hour dinners: "The dinner will run from 6:30-9:30pm" (2) and "private dining room at Kokkari... 6:30-9:30pm" (7, 21, 61).

dimensions.name: Template-ness / mail-merge residue
dimensions.definition: Visible evidence the email is a mass template: broken or lazy merge fields, generic swap-in structure where only name/company changes, and recycled boilerplate blocks. Judged per-email from artifacts in the text (duplication across the pack corroborates but isn't required).
dimensions.variation_seen: High residue: "Hi ," (5); "Assuming you and the Christian team will be in Nashville" (63); the signature artifact "Email: charlotte@encord.com: mailto:youremail@encord.com" (13, 32, 48, 88, 94); the verbatim block "Bit of context on Encord...we're a computer vision scale-up (recently raised a $30M Series B)" appearing in 8+ emails. Low residue: bespoke notes like "Winnie brought me up to speed on your chat at CVPR & excited to explore potential ways we can help the Disney team" (1) or the hand-written reconnect to Ravin citing "congrats on the partnership with Five Sigma!" (71).

dimensions.name: Mechanical polish (grammar, typos, formatting)
dimensions.definition: Freedom from grammatical errors, typos, malformed sentences, duplicated legal footers, and raw tracking-link clutter that make the email look careless.
dimensions.variation_seen: Errors are frequent and graded: the recurring "if you're be open to a 30-minute chat" (3, 13, 22, 27, 97), "Muck like them... building models in house with automated training data pipelines become top of mind" and "onboarded quick a few of your peers" (85), "unfies a significant amount of the ML tech stake" (64), "private dinning room" (31), "NVIDA GTC" (33, 70). Clean examples read flawlessly end-to-end, e.g. the Zurich dinner invite "It'll be an informal, open-format evening - no slides or pitches, just great food and conversation" (23, 49) or email 50.

dimensions.name: Brevity and scannability
dimensions.definition: Length and structural economy: word count of the body, paragraph size, and whether structure (short paragraphs, bullets) lets a skimmer extract who/why/ask in seconds.
dimensions.variation_seen: High economy: email 47 is three sentences total ("Great to see that you were exploring Encord... Let me know if you have any questions"), and 42/90 are a single short paragraph ("Quick note to ask - will you be attending GTC Paris this year..."). Low: email 67 runs ~180 words with a three-bullet feature list and buries the ask ("Not sure if your team has any plans to reevaluate their data infra stack this year? Either way..."), and 2 spends four dense paragraphs before the ask.

dimensions.name: Peer-to-peer vs. salesy tone
dimensions.definition: Whether the register is a collegial exchange (trading notes, asking for feedback, low pressure) or a pitch with urgency/scarcity pressure and product-brochure phrasing. Judged from wording, not intent.
dimensions.variation_seen: Peer register: "keen to trade notes & get your candid feedback on what we're building" (25), "no slides or pitches, just great food and conversation" (82). Salesy register: "That's where the Encord platform comes in. Designed to streamline data management and accelerate model development" (20), and scarcity pressure "les places sont limitées et attribuées selon le principe du premier arrivé, premier servi" [seats limited, first come first served] (32, 38); softer pressure variants like "We're capping the attendance to 40 guests - so let me know if you can make it!" (73) sit in between.

corpus_observations: The pack splits into two dominant genres — conference-adjacent event invites (dinners, mixers, panels at ProMat, CVPR, NeurIPS, ICCV, ISC West; roughly 40 emails) and direct cold pitches asking for a 20-30 minute call or a coffee — plus about 10-12 emails that are not true first-touches (rescheduling notes, 'we're on the call now', post-demo follow-ups, doc links). Nearly all follow a shared skeleton: personalized hook, peer/customer proof, an 'in case you're not familiar with Encord' boilerplate paragraph, then the ask — so quality variance lives mostly in how well each slot is filled, not in structure. Template reuse is heavy and visible: several bodies are byte-identical across recipients, and mail-merge artifacts (a blank 'Hi ,', 'youremail@encord.com' fragments, a duplicated company paragraph) appear alongside genuinely bespoke, well-researched notes referencing the recipient's specific models, talks, or funding rounds. Polish varies sharply within the same sender pool, from flawless invites to emails with collapsed bullet formatting, 'diver safety' for 'driver safety', and 'if you're be open' constructions. Social proof is universal but ranges from tightly vertical peer lists to the same three marquee logos pasted regardless of the recipient's industry.

The pack mixes several outreach genres: cold first-touch intros pegged to a trigger event, event/dinner invites (roughly a quarter of the pack, e.g. the Aerlume Seattle dinner appears ~6 times with only the opening line swapped), conference meeting requests (CVPR/GTC/NeurIPS/ISC West), post-demo and post-call follow-ups, and website-visitor re-engagement notes; a handful are not really prospect outreach at all (a venue inquiry, an internal intro, a reply to a vendor). Template reuse is heavy and visible: "demo - real workspace" recurs verbatim 4 times, "Plan for CVPR" 5 times, and boilerplate blocks like "Bit of context on Encord...we're a computer vision scale-up (recently raised a $30M Series B)" repeat word-for-word across senders. Mail-merge failures are common and conspicuous: "Hi ," with a blank name, "Will you and the name team", "working with companies like name", "theAdvantis team", and signature artifacts like "Email: charlotte@encord.com: mailto:youremail@encord.com". At the other extreme, some emails show genuinely specific research ("Congratulations on completing the first unmanned, deep-water cable route survey", "I saw your facial recognition model was featured on the NIST leaderboard") and bespoke content (China/VPN contracting details, FDA-traceability arguments referencing the prospect's actual tool, itk-snap). Nearly every email name-drops customers, so what varies is not the presence of social proof but how well the named customers match the recipient's domain. Length runs from two sentences to five dense paragraphs, and asks range from concrete offered time slots to open-ended "Open to learning more?".

dimensions.name: Recipient-specific research depth
dimensions.definition: How much the email demonstrates verifiable knowledge of this specific recipient or their company — a named announcement, publication, talk, hire, award, or mutual contact — versus generic or absent personalization. Judged only on what is claimed in the text and how specific/checkable the claim is.

corpus_observations: The pack is dominated by three recurring genres: exclusive event invites (roughly 35-40 dinner/mixer/happy-hour invitations tied to conferences like CVPR, NeurIPS, CES, Actuate, ISC West, all following a fixed formula of venue + capped guest count + name-dropped attendee list + 'In case Encord is new to you...' paragraph), conference coffee-meeting requests, and cold pitches anchored on a named customer case study ('We recently onboarded Motive/Woven/Entrust...'). A meaningful minority are inbound-lead follow-ups ('thank you for your interest in Encord') and a handful are actually mid-thread replies rather than true first touches (#9, #38, #46, #54, #56, #80, #95). Template reuse is heavy and visible: several emails are verbatim duplicates with only the company name swapped, and slot-fill artifacts (empty 'Hi ,', uncapitalized 'shell team', signature placeholders like youremail@encord.com) surface repeatedly. Social proof is near-universal — almost every email names customers (Boston Dynamics, Woven by Toyota, Synthesia, Physical Intelligence) — so what varies is its sector relevance, not its presence. Mechanical quality is uneven for a commercial team: typos ('vvideo', 'train training', 'NeuriPS'), collapsed bullet formatting, and garbled sentences appear in a nontrivial fraction. The best emails combine a checkable trigger, a domain-specific pain hypothesis, and a dated low-friction ask; the weakest are generic platform descriptions with 'Open to learning more?'
